title: Reading Complex Texts
description: Read and analyze complex literary and informational texts with close reading strategies.
objectives: Apply close reading strategies
Analyze complex syntax and diction
Draw inferences supported by textual evidence

lessons.title: Close Reading
lessons.content: Close reading involves careful, repeated analysis of how a text creates meaning.
examples: Annotate as you read: underline key passages, circle unfamiliar words, mark patterns
First read: what happens? Second read: how is it written? Third read: what does it mean?
Find the 'moments of friction' — places where the text surprises or confuses you

lessons.title: Textual Evidence
lessons.content: All claims about a text must be supported with specific evidence.
examples: Strong: 'Holden Caulfield's repeated use of the word 'phony' reveals his disillusionment with adult society (Salinger, 2)','Weak: 'The character seems unhappy'

title: Literary Analysis Essay
description: Write a formal literary analysis essay with a thesis, textual evidence, and analysis.
objectives: Write a sophisticated, arguable thesis
Integrate quotations smoothly (ICE: introduce, cite, explain)
Develop analysis beyond plot summary

lessons.title: The Literary Analysis Thesis
lessons.content: A literary analysis thesis makes a specific, arguable claim about how a text works.
examples: Weak: 'In Lord of the Flies, the boys become savage'
Strong: 'Golding uses the conch shell as a symbol of democratic order to show how quickly civilization collapses when authority is no longer enforced by force'

lessons.title: ICE — Integrate Evidence
lessons.content: Quote integration: Introduce the quote, Cite it, then Explain its significance.
examples: Introduce: 'Golding emphasizes this collapse when...'
Cite: '...the conch shattered into a thousand white fragments' (181)
Explain: 'The physical destruction of the conch symbolizes the final dissolution of democratic order on the island'

title: Informational Reading — Multiple Perspectives
description: Analyze how different authors treat the same topic; evaluate conflicting evidence.
objectives: Compare accounts with different perspectives
Evaluate credibility and bias
Synthesize conflicting information

lessons.title: Multiple Perspectives
lessons.content: On any complex topic, credible sources may reach different conclusions.
examples: Two historians may interpret the same event differently based on their sources
Identify: What evidence does each author use? What are their assumptions?
Neither text need be 'wrong' — complexity is normal in real inquiry

lessons.title: Evaluating Bias
lessons.content: All texts have a perspective; bias isn't always intentional.
examples: Check: Who funded this study?
Are counterarguments addressed honestly?
Does the author have relevant expertise?

title: Research — Extended Project
description: Complete an extended research project with annotated bibliography and formal paper.
objectives: Develop an original research question
Create an annotated bibliography
Write a well-organized research paper with proper MLA citations

lessons.title: The Research Question
lessons.content: A great research question is specific, debatable, and researchable.
examples: Too broad: 'Is climate change real?'
Too narrow: 'What is the average temperature in Phoenix in July 2019?'
Just right: 'How has climate change affected wildfire frequency in California over the past 30 years?'

lessons.title: Annotated Bibliography
lessons.content: Each source gets a citation plus a paragraph summarizing and evaluating it.
examples: Summary: What does this source argue or show?
Evaluation: How credible is it? What is its potential bias?
Usefulness: How does it relate to your research question?

title: Grammar — Advanced Usage and Style
description: Master advanced grammar for precise, effective writing.
objectives: Use active vs. passive voice appropriately
Avoid common errors: dangling modifiers, faulty parallelism
Vary sentence structure for rhetorical effect

lessons.title: Active vs. Passive Voice
lessons.content: Active voice is direct and clear; passive has its uses but can obscure meaning.
examples: Passive: 'The ball was kicked by John.'
Active: 'John kicked the ball.' (clearer, more direct)
Appropriate passive: 'Mistakes were made' (when actor is unknown or irrelevant)

lessons.title: Parallel Structure
lessons.content: Items in a series must have the same grammatical form.
examples: Wrong: 'She liked reading, to swim, and dances'
Correct: 'She liked reading, swimming, and dancing'
Wrong: 'He is talented, hardworking, and has a lot of patience'
Correct: 'He is talented, hardworking, and patient'

title: Dystopian Literature
description: Analyze the dystopian genre through major works and the social critiques they encode.
objectives: Define dystopian fiction and its conventions
Analyze how dystopias critique real societies
Compare two dystopian texts

lessons.title: Dystopia Conventions
lessons.content: Dystopian fiction presents a nightmarish future society to critique present trends.
examples: Total government control (1984, The Giver)
Loss of individual freedom, enforced conformity
Technology used to oppress (surveillance, propaganda)
Often features a protagonist who begins to question the system

lessons.title: Social Critique
lessons.content: Dystopias always comment on real fears and tendencies in contemporary society.
examples: 1984 (1949): critiques Stalinist totalitarianism and surveillance
The Hunger Games: critiques media exploitation and wealth inequality
Handmaid's Tale: critiques patriarchy and religious extremism

title: Speeches and Rhetoric
description: Analyze great speeches for rhetorical strategies and craft; write and deliver a speech.
objectives: Analyze rhetorical strategies in historic speeches
Write a persuasive speech with ethos, pathos, logos
Deliver a speech with effective techniques

lessons.title: Analyzing Great Speeches
lessons.content: Great speeches combine rhetorical appeals with powerful language.
examples: MLK's 'I Have a Dream': anaphora ('I have a dream that...'), vivid metaphor, emotional appeal
Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: parallel structure, elevated diction, emotional pathos
Malala's UN Speech: ethos (personal experience), logos (statistics), pathos (urgency)

title: Vocabulary — Figurative and Connotative Language
description: Analyze how figurative and connotative language shapes meaning and tone.
objectives: Analyze extended metaphors
Interpret symbolism in literary texts
Evaluate how word choice creates tone

lessons.title: Extended Metaphors
lessons.content: A metaphor sustained across a text creates layered meaning.
examples: 'Hope is the thing with feathers' (Emily Dickinson) — hope is compared to a bird throughout
'All the world's a stage' (Shakespeare) — people as actors, life as a play

lessons.title: Symbolism
lessons.content: Symbols are objects, characters, or events that represent larger ideas.
examples: The green light in Gatsby: the American Dream, unattainable hope
The conch in Lord of the Flies: democratic order and civilization
The mockingbird in To Kill a Mockingbird: innocence destroyed by evil

title: Multimedia and Digital Literacy
description: Create and analyze multimodal texts; evaluate digital information critically.
objectives: Analyze how visuals and text work together
Create a multimedia presentation or documentary
Evaluate digital sources using advanced criteria

lessons.title: Multimodal Texts
lessons.content: Modern communication combines words, images, sound, and video.
examples: A documentary uses interview, narration, b-roll footage, and music together
Websites layer text, images, hyperlinks, and interactive elements
Analyze each element: What does the image add that words don't? How does music shape emotional response?

lessons.title: Digital Citizenship
lessons.content: Responsible digital citizenship includes creating and sharing responsibly.
examples: Understand copyright: you can't use others' images/music without permission
Cite digital sources; use Creative Commons-licensed images
Think before posting: digital footprints are permanent

title: Independent Reading and Reflection
description: Synthesize learning through sustained independent reading and reflective writing.
objectives: Read a self-selected challenging text
Write a reflective reader's essay
Connect reading to personal growth and worldview

lessons.title: Choosing Challenging Texts
lessons.content: Reading above your comfort level builds skills and expands worldview.
examples: Choose books that push you: unfamiliar settings, complex characters, challenging ideas
A little struggle is productive — if you understand every sentence immediately, the book may not be challenging enough

lessons.title: Reflective Reading Essay
lessons.content: A reflective essay connects the text to your own thinking and growth.
examples: How did reading this book change how you see the world?
What question did it leave you with?
Connect ideas from the book to other texts, courses, or your own experience
